nameStory: The "rock whitewash" name comes from its whitish, crusty appearance that looks like someone splashed whitewash paint across rock surfaces. The alternate name "eggshell rock blaze" refers to both its eggshell-like texture and the way it creates blazing white patches that stand out dramatically against dark rock faces.
description: Rock whitewash is a crusty lichen that grows directly on rock surfaces, forming thin, whitish patches that look like dried paint or plaster. This crustose lichen spreads in irregular patches across stone, creating a bumpy, textured surface. It's typically several inches across when mature, though individual patches can merge to cover larger areas of rock.

idTips.label: Rock-dwelling habitat
idTips.description: Always grows directly on bare rock surfaces, never on bark or soil - if you're not looking at stone, it's not rock whitewash

idTips.label: Crusty white texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and chalky like dried plaster when you run your finger across it, with a distinctly bumpy, granular surface

idTips.label: Whitish-gray color
idTips.description: Ranges from bright white to pale gray, often with a slightly dirty or weathered appearance that distinguishes it from fresh paint

idTips.label: Irregular patches
idTips.description: Grows in uneven, blob-like patches rather than perfect circles, with edges that fade gradually into the rock surface

idTips.label: Blemished surface
idTips.description: Close inspection reveals tiny dark dots or blemishes scattered across the white surface, like freckles on pale skin

habitat: Look for rock whitewash on exposed rock faces, cliffs, and large boulders throughout New England's forests and rocky areas. It prefers natural stone surfaces in partially shaded to moderately sunny locations, often alongside other rock-dwelling lichens.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as winter debris clears away from rock faces. Fresh growth may appear brighter white after spring rains wash away accumulated dirt.
seasonality.summer: Most active growing season, though changes are subtle. The lichen may appear slightly more vibrant during humid periods.
seasonality.fall: Remains clearly visible as leaves drop, often becoming one of the most noticeable organisms on bare rock surfaces.
seasonality.winter: Easily spotted against snow-covered or frost-covered rocks. The whitish patches stand out dramatically in the stark winter landscape.

funFact: This lichen was only officially recognized as its own species in 2017, meaning countless nature lovers had been looking at an unnamed organism for decades without knowing they were seeing something scientifically undescribed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative whitewash lichen, but rock whitewash exclusively grows on stone while whitewash lichen typically grows on tree bark. Memory trick: "Rock whitewash rocks on rocks" - if it's on bark, it's the other species.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with actual whitewash paint that might have been applied to old stone foundations or walls - real rock whitewash lichen has a more irregular, organic appearance and will show those characteristic tiny dark blemishes when you look closely.
compareHints: Rock whitewash differs from its close relative whitewash lichen primarily by habitat - rock whitewash grows exclusively on stone surfaces while whitewash lichen prefers tree bark. Both share the characteristic whitish, crusty appearance and similar blemished surface texture, but their substrate preference makes identification straightforward once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Whitewash Lichen differs from its close relative Rock Whitewash by its strong preference for tree bark over rocky surfaces.
